title: From skills to subagents
tagline: Tell a skill from a subagent and define a subagent's six key fields.
summary: Aishwarya recaps where CLAUDE.md, skills and docs live (user, project and team level), then introduces subagents as the second tier of automation, using a teacher and student agents analogy to show why each subagent gets its own context window. Hamza builds a CLAUDE.md from an empty folder and runs the SEO writer subagent system live on a student's topic, producing a researched article for about $0.60. The session ends with the six fields of a subagent file and how a subagent differs from a skill and from an agent team.

questions.q: What's the actual difference between a skill and a subagent?
questions.answer:
Aishwarya's short version: a skill is one repeatable task with one prompt, while a subagent takes one delegated piece of a bigger task that has been split into subtasks [1]. A subagent can call a skill, but only when its piece of the work needs one [2].

The bigger practical difference is the context window. A skill runs inside your main chat, so every turn fills that chat up. A subagent runs independently with a fresh context, and the main agent just collects its output, "almost like a postmaster" [3]. On top of that, a subagent can set its own model, tools and memory.

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: for a skill. one repeatable task, one prompt, super prompt, being able to complete as one task, one skill, versus a sub-agent, think of it as any sort of a task that can be delegated

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: Skill, It's used for a task. Sub-agent is used for one of the decompositions of a main task into multiple subtasks, and the subagent can also call a skill…

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: Calls that sub-agent and makes it run independently, which means your main charts context window is not being used… the main agent's only job is to, almost like a postmaster, collect the output

questions.q: What do I put in a subagent's markdown file?
questions.answer:
Aishwarya walks through six fields, the first two being the same front matter a skill has [1]:

- **name** and **description**. The main agent reads the description to decide which subagent gets a task, so make it specific.
- **model**. The subagent runs on this model rather than the main chat's, so research can use Opus while a summarizer uses Haiku [2].
- **tools**, such as web search or Brave MCP for research, or Read and Grep for a reviewer.
- **memory**, a file the subagent adds to on each run.
- **skills**, an optional pointer to an existing skill.

None of the six is mandatory [3]. The starter repo's code reviewer agent shows the format.

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: which is the name and the description, what we call as the front matter for the skill file, right? That part remains, so, for summation, there are, like, six important sections.

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: the research sub-agent can actually run on one of the most frontier models, like Opus… The summarizer can run on Haiko, because you don't need, like, a super powerful model

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: So the six fields that you see here. are actually what that matters the most, but it is not a mandatory that your sub-agent should always have all of these things.

questions.q: What happened in the live SEO writer demo, and what did the run cost?
questions.answer:
Hamza took a topic from the chat (Tarik's question on how AI changes the startup ecosystem), reframed it for a non-technical founder entering the EU market, and hit run. The SEO writer is a system of subagents, including research, editorial and evaluation agents [1], and Hamza left it alone while it worked [2].

When the class came back to it, the run had taken 7 steps, cost about $0.60 and generated 34,000 tokens [3]. The article, on AI tools for non-technical founders entering the EU market, included images and an example that Hamza says it found without being prompted. Aishwarya used the run to show how one request splits into research, an outline, writing, images and a humanizing check.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: And there is a whole agent… sub-agent ecosystem. This is… that we run, you know, there's a research agent, there's an editorial agent, so-and-so things that run, there's an evaluation agent that runs.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: I just wanted you guys to see that it started running, and I will not change anything in it. I will not do anything to it myself. I will let the whole Agent ecosystem run it fun.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: it took about 9 steps to run, 7 steps, and it chose to run on 7 steps… the entire article took 0.6 cents, or sorry.6 dollars to write. The total number of tokens that we generated is 34,000.

questions.q: How do I decide between subagents and an agent team?
questions.answer:
Aishwarya boils it down to one question: do the tasks need to talk to each other, or can they run on their own and combine at the end [1]? If they can run independently, subagents fit. Agent teams, covered in the next module, are for work where agents talk to each other as they go.

Shashank asked whether passing research on to a writer makes it a team. Aishwarya's answer was no: the output moves sequentially, but no agent talks to another mid-way [2].

Hamza's analogy is that a subagent is one freelancer, while an agent team is hiring a full team [3]. Aishwarya adds that you hand a freelancer the job and wait for a summary, while a team keeps building on each other's input.

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: Do every task actually talk to each other, or can these tasks actually run independently and just come together at the end to combine all the output into one?

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: it's not about the output being dependent, it's about the two agents being able to talk to each other… the output is being passed sequentially as steps, but that does not mean that one agent is actually having to talk…

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: There's a difference between agent team and sub-agent. Sub-agents can just be independent. You can have one freelancer. But agent is actually hiring a full team.

questions.q: What's the difference between a user-level and a project-level CLAUDE.md?
questions.answer:
Aishwarya explains that CLAUDE.md works at more than one level [1]. A user-level CLAUDE.md sits in the .claude folder of your user profile, describes you, and carries over to every project you create. A project-level CLAUDE.md describes one project, which can be your own pet project or a GitHub repo your whole team shares [2]. The two can coexist, and Aishwarya notes this scoping is one of the trickiest areas in the certification exam.

Skills follow the same split. Hamza's beautiful HTML skill lives in his user folder, so it works in any project. To promote a project skill, ask Claude to register it as a slash command and it moves to the user level [3].

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: cloud.md is acting at multiple levels… there can exist a .clot folder and a clot.md file, which can have definitions of the user that is you, and that automatically gets carried over to different projects

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: there is also a project-level Claw.md that you can create, which carries a definition of that specific project… or it can also be the GitHub repo that your entire team is using

citations.speaker: Aishwarya Ashok
citations.quote: turn the skill into a slash command, and that automatically puts that skill into the user-level, elevation already. So all you have to do is just ask Claude to say, register the skill into a slash command.
